title: The Palace on Lochias to the Sealed Tomb: the last Ptolemy, two Romans, and a kingdom held on a will
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace on Lochias: a daughter born to the Flute-Player
stops.date_confidence: Year most likely 69 BC, possibly late 70. No ancient source records the birth at all, so the day is unknown and defaulted to 01-01 and the mother is unnamed. Place is inference from the dynasty's residence, not from a document. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Alexandria palace pin, the promontory of Lochias, inherited byte-identical from julius_caesar.journey.json; the research pool's own 31.2136/29.8992 falls in open water in the middle of the Eastern Harbour and is not used.
stops.campa: A third daughter is born to Ptolemy XII, whom Alexandria calls Auletes, the Flute-Player, a king who plays the aulos in public procession and borrows from Roman financiers to keep a throne Rome could take whenever it chose to. The house he heads descends from a Macedonian officer of Alexander and has held Egypt for two hundred and fifty years from Alexandria, a city the official formula places next to Egypt rather than in it. Her mother's name is not recorded. Neither is the day.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Alexandria', on the Royal Palaces at Lochias and their submersion
suggested_refs: The submerged Lochias promontory, the modern Silsileh, and the excavated island of Antirhodos
alexander.journey.json

stops.name: Alexandria, the Museum quarter: the tongue of many strings
stops.date_confidence: No source dates her education or names a teacher. 58 BC orders the stop within the segment only, falling in the years her father spent in exile appealing to Rome. The account of her languages is Plutarch, Life of Antony 27, written roughly a century and a half after her death and reporting what was said of her rather than any contemporary record. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from strabo.journey.json, the atlas pin for the Museum and Library quarter.
stops.campa: The Ptolemies keep a Museum and a Library beside the palace and salaried scholars to go with them, and the daughters of the house are taught there as the sons are. What Alexandria makes of her is a linguist. Plutarch, writing a century and a half later and setting down what was said of her rather than any record of her schooling, has her dealing with Ethiopians, Troglodytes, Hebrews, Arabians, Syrians, Medes and Parthians without sending for an interpreter. She also learns Egyptian, which no one of her line had done in two and a half centuries of governing Egyptians.
stops.quote: her tongue, like an instrument of many strings, she could readily turn to whatever language she pleased, so that in her interviews with Barbarians she very seldom had need of an interpreter
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 27, trans. Bernadotte Perrin (Loeb Classical Library), LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The Museum and Library of Alexandria in the Brucheion quarter, inland from the harbour front

stops.name: Dendera, the Temple of Hathor: regent at her father's side
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra': 'On 31 May 52 BC, Cleopatra was made a regent to Ptolemy XII, as indicated by an inscription in the Temple of Hathor at Dendera'; Wikipedia, 'Ptolemy XII Auletes' states it independently. The research pool tagged this as reconstruction; corrected here to attested, since two articles state it without hedging. Whether she travelled to Dendera herself for the act is not stated anywhere and should not be assumed. Coordinate matches Wikipedia, 'Dendera Temple complex' (26.14167/32.67028).
stops.campa: Some four hundred and fifty miles up the river from Alexandria, on the temple of Hathor at Dendera, a dated line puts her beside her father as regent: the thirty-first of May. She is seventeen or eighteen. Auletes has been restored to his throne by a Roman army paid for with Roman loans, and he is failing. Naming a daughter regent settles the succession while he can still order it. The record of it is cut by an Egyptian priesthood, in the pharaonic idiom the court at Alexandria mostly ignores.
suggested_refs: The rear exterior wall of the Temple of Hathor at Dendera, carrying the late Ptolemaic relief of Cleopatra and Caesarion making offering

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: the will that makes Rome the executor
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the research pool, which gave March 51 BC as the death month. Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra' and 'Ptolemy XII Auletes' give only 'some time before 22 March 51 BC', a terminus ante quem derived from the Buchis-bull stela and not a recorded date. 03-01 is used here to order the segment only. The clause making the Roman people executors of the will is attested: 'he made the people of Rome executors of his will.'
stops.campa: Ptolemy XII dies some time before the twenty-second of March; no source records the month. His will divides the throne between his eighteen-year-old daughter and her brother Ptolemy XIII, who is about ten and comes with a set of guardians. It also names the Roman people as its executors. So the richest kingdom left standing in the Mediterranean, which no army has taken, now holds its crown by a document whose enforcement lies with the Senate. She is queen from that day, jointly, on those terms.
suggested_refs: The Buchis stela of 51 BC, which supplies the terminus ante quem for Auletes's death

segments.name: Sole Queen, Then No Queen At All

stops.name: Hermonthis, the Bucheum: the queen rows up to install the bull
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra' records 'her voyage to Hermonthis, near Thebes, to install a new sacred Buchis bull' as an early act of the reign, dated by the Buchis stela to 22 March 51 BC. Coordinate is the Bucheum necropolis at Armant.
stops.campa: One of the first acts of the new reign is a river voyage. She goes up to Hermonthis, near Thebes, to install a new Buchis bull, the living animal in which the god is held to reside, and the priests cut a stela recording that the queen came in person; it is that stela which fixes the date of her father's death. Upper Egypt is where the dynasty's authority runs thinnest and where the temple priesthoods run strongest. She arrives in front of them as pharaoh, not as the Macedonian in Alexandria who signs their tax orders.
suggested_refs: The Bucheum at Armant and its series of dated burial stelae for the Buchis bulls

stops.name: The Faiyum: Thea Philopator, and no brother named
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to place. The dedication is dated 2 July 51 BC but the exact findspot within the Faiyum is uncertain, so the coordinate is the nome capital and not a confirmed site; the relief may also be recut from an earlier male ruler's image. That official documents by late August 51 name her alone is separately attested (Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra', 29 August 51 BC).
stops.campa: A dedication out of the Faiyum names her Thea Philopator, the Father-Loving Goddess, and names nobody else. By the end of August the official documents of the kingdom are dated by her regnal year alone, with her brother's name simply left out of them. The erasure is done in the chancery and not in the palace, and it does not hold. Ptolemy XIII has Pothinus the eunuch, Achillas the general and Theodotus the rhetorician behind him. Between them they hold the boy, and through the boy the guard and the city.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra' (fetched), on the sole-rule documents of 29 August 51 BC
suggested_refs: Faiyum epigraphy of the early sole reign, including the question of recut earlier reliefs

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: the Gabiniani sent back in chains
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an episode (Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra'); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01-01. Her motive is reconstruction: no source states why she chose to hand the killers over rather than shield them.
stops.campa: The soldiers Gabinius left behind when he restored her father have married locally, taken Egyptian pay, and stopped answering to Rome. When two sons of the proconsul Bibulus come to recruit them for the Syrian war, the Gabiniani kill them. Cleopatra has the killers arrested and sent in chains to Bibulus for judgment. He declines to try them and refers the matter to the Senate instead. Nothing comes back to her from Rome for it. The Gabiniani are the only standing army in Alexandria, and within the year the court has driven her out of the city.
suggested_refs: The Gabiniani, the Roman garrison left in Egypt in 55 BC and progressively naturalised there

stops.name: Ashkelon: a free city's mint strikes her portrait
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dated bronze coinage of Ashkelon in her name is standard modern numismatic scholarship (Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography, among others); no primary coin catalogue was reachable in preparing this file. No narrative source places her inside the city, and the stop stands for the exile years in Roman Syria generally. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Ashkelon on the Philistine coast is a free city with its own mint, and in these years it strikes dated bronze carrying her portrait. She has been pushed first into the Thebaid and then over the frontier, and she is somewhere in this country raising a mercenary army out of the Syrian levies. A city that is not hers is putting her face on its money at the one moment she has no mint of her own. The coins are the whole of the evidence for these months. No narrative source puts her inside the walls.
sources: Modern numismatic reconstruction as summarised in the research pool; primary coin catalogue not reachable
suggested_refs: The dated Ashkelon bronze issues in Cleopatra's name, 49/48 BC

stops.name: Pelusium, the camp at the frontier: an army raised abroad, and a head kept
stops.date_confidence: Her camp outside Pelusium is attested (Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra': 'camped outside Pelousion in the eastern Nile Delta'). Pompey's murder is attested to 28 September 48 BC. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 31.0546/32.533 to Wikipedia, 'Pelusium' (31°02'30"N 32°32'42"E = 31.04167/32.54500), about 1.8 km away. She is in the region, not at the killing; no source places her on the shore.
stops.campa: She brings her hired army down to Pelusium, the fortress that guards the eastern road into Egypt, and camps opposite her brother's forces, and neither side moves. Then Pompey arrives by sea, beaten at Pharsalus, expecting the hospitality Egypt owes the man who put her father back on his throne. Ptolemy XIII's advisers reason that a dead Pompey cannot reproach anyone and that Caesar will be grateful. They kill him in a small boat within sight of his wife on the deck, on the twenty-eighth of September, and keep the head.
sources: cicero.journey.json, stop 'Dyrrachium - Pharsalus, the battle he does not fight'
suggested_refs: The silted site of Pelusium, some 30 km south-east of modern Port Said
cicero.journey.json

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: carried in past the guards
stops.date_confidence: Caesar's arrival in early October 48 BC is attested; the day is approximate. The smuggling is Plutarch's, in the Life of Caesar, and Apollodorus the Sicilian is named there; the bedding sack is the ancient detail and the rolled carpet is a later retelling. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Alexandria palace pin, matching julius_caesar.journey.json byte-identical.
stops.campa: Caesar lands four days after the murder, is handed Pompey's head and signet ring, and installs himself in the palace as arbitrator between the two Ptolemies, which is not a thing anybody has invited him to do. Cleopatra is outside the city with an army that cannot get past her brother's lines. So she comes by water at night with one man, Apollodorus the Sicilian, and is carried in through the guards inside a roll of bedding. Plutarch says the trick was the first thing about her that took him. The retellings turn the bedding into a carpet.
sources: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 49, as summarised in World History Encyclopedia, 'Cleopatra VII' (the Penelope page truncated before ch. 49 and was not read to the end)
julius_caesar.journey.json, stop 'Alexandria: besieged in the palace quarter'
suggested_refs: julius_caesar.journey.json

stops.name: Alexandria, the Great Harbour: the fire among the book stores
stops.date_confidence: The Alexandrian War is attested; the fire is reported inconsistently across the ancient accounts and no ancient source establishes damage to the Library as an institution. Month is approximate, the siege running through the winter of 48/47. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Great Harbour pin, inherited byte-identical from bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json. The Latin Bellum Alexandrinum was not fetched in preparing this file.
stops.campa: The Alexandrians rise against the Roman garrison and Achillas brings the army up from Pelusium. Arsinoe IV slips out of the palace and is proclaimed queen by the besiegers, which makes three living claimants inside one city. Caesar, cut off in the palace quarter with too few men, fires the ships at their moorings to keep the harbour open, and the fire runs up the docks and takes warehouses of books stored along them. What it did or did not do to the Library the ancient accounts do not agree on, and none of them was written by anyone who was there.
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum (anonymous, Corpus Caesarianum), not fetched
julius_caesar.journey.json, which records the same fire from Caesar's side
suggested_refs: The later tradition that the Library of Alexandria burned in 48 BC, which the ancient evidence does not establish for the main institution

stops.name: The Nile delta: the brother drowned in the river
stops.date_confidence: Date corrected from the pool's loose '-0047-01'. Wikipedia, 'Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator': he 'reportedly drowned on 13 January 47 BC while attempting to cross the Nile river' after the Battle of the Nile. The same source flags that whether he was fleeing or seeking negotiations is uncertain. The battle site is not securely located; the coordinate is an approximate point in the eastern delta and not a landmark. The recovery of his gilded corselet is reported, not documented.
stops.campa: Reinforcements come down from Syria and Judaea, the siege breaks, and the war ends out on the river. Ptolemy XIII, thirteen years old, drowns crossing the Nile on the thirteenth of January. Whether he was running from the defeat or trying to reach a parley the sources do not settle, and what was recovered from the water, they say, was his gilded corselet. Cleopatra is queen of Egypt with a Roman army in her capital. Caesar pairs her with the surviving brother, Ptolemy XIV, about twelve, and leaves three legions behind him when he goes.
suggested_refs: The Battle of the Nile, January 47 BC, whose site has never been fixed

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: a son named Ptolemy Caesar
stops.date_confidence: The birth is attested; the date of 23 June is proposed from Egyptian evidence and is not universally accepted. The paternity was politically disputed in Rome in her lifetime and cannot be established from any source. Caesar's departure in spring or early summer 47 BC for the Pontic campaign is attested (Livius.org).
stops.campa: A son is born in the palace and she names him Ptolemy Caesar. Alexandria calls him Caesarion. She presents him publicly as Caesar's, has him shown on Egyptian temple walls beside her in the pharaonic manner, and puts him where Egypt will see him. Caesar never acknowledges the boy at Rome and never mentions him in his will. The date given for the birth, the twenty-third of June, is proposed from Egyptian evidence and is not accepted by everyone. By the time the child is a month old his father has sailed for Pontus.
sources: julius_caesar.journey.json, stop 'Alexandria: at the tomb of Alexander', March 47 BC
suggested_refs: julius_caesar.journey.json
The Dendera relief of Cleopatra and Caesarion, among the few monumental images naming him as co-ruler

segments.name: Rome, the Gardens Across the Tiber

stops.name: Rome, the Horti Caesaris: a queen lodged across the river
stops.date_confidence: The residence in Caesar's gardens on the west bank and the Senate's recognition of her and Ptolemy XIV as friends and allies of the Roman people are attested. Month and day of arrival unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the west-bank Horti Caesaris placement carried over from the interlock reading; the pool's other candidate, 41.8913/12.4692, sits closer to the river. Cicero's letters are cited from attalus.org's Shuckburgh text, whose letter numbering was not cross-checked against Shackleton Bailey.
stops.campa: She comes to Rome with Ptolemy XIV, the child, and a court, and is put up in Caesar's own gardens on the far bank of the Tiber rather than in any public residence. It is a scandal and a convenience at once. The Senate registers her and her brother as friends and allies of the Roman people. Cicero, who has dealings with her circle and is promised books by her agent Ammonius that never come, records what the Roman governing class makes of the arrangement in a single line to Atticus.
stops.quote: I detest the queen; and the guarantor of her promises, Ammonius, knows I have good reason to do so.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus, Book 15, trans. Evelyn Shuckburgh, attalus.org; written after her stay in Rome, 44 BC
sources: Cicero, Letters to Atticus 14-15 (attalus.org, Shuckburgh translation)
cicero.journey.json (absence check: no Rome scene with her residence appears in that file)
suggested_refs: cicero.journey.json
The Horti Caesaris on the west bank of the Tiber, bequeathed to the Roman people in Caesar's will

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Venus Genetrix: gilded beside the goddess
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia, 'Temple of Venus Genetrix': dedicated 26 September 46 BC on the last day of Caesar's fourfold triumph, and describing the object as 'a controversial golden statue of Queen Cleopatra as the goddess Isis'. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 41.8925/12.4853 and inherited byte-identical from julius_caesar.journey.json, which carries the same stop from Caesar's side.
stops.campa: On the last day of his fourfold triumph Caesar dedicates the temple of Venus Genetrix at the head of his new forum, to the goddess from whom his line claims descent. What stands inside, beside the goddess, is a gilded statue of the living queen of Egypt, who is lodged across the river with her brother and her son. Rome will see a foreign woman put up in a temple of the Roman state by a man in his fourth dictatorship. Alexandria will see Isis and Venus made one, which is how she has presented herself at home since her accession.
sources: julius_caesar.journey.json, stop 'Rome, the Temple of Venus Genetrix: the goddess in the family'
suggested_refs: julius_caesar.journey.json
The Forum Iulium and its surviving foundations

stops.name: Rome, the Ides of March: a will that does not name her son
stops.date_confidence: The assassination and the terms of the will are attested. That she was in Rome at the time is attested; where in the city she was lodged in these particular weeks is not recorded, so the coordinate is a general city point rather than a site. Her departure for Egypt in the following months is attested, the exact date is not.
stops.campa: She is still in the city on the fifteenth of March when Caesar is killed in the Senate. The will is opened and read out: it adopts his great-nephew Gaius Octavius and it says nothing about her, and nothing about the boy across the river whom she has named Ptolemy Caesar. Where exactly she was lodged in these weeks nobody wrote down. She stays about a month, long enough to see whether the assassins or the heirs will hold the city, and then takes ship for Alexandria.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius, as listed in the research pool's source apparatus
suggested_refs: The adoption of Gaius Octavius in Caesar's will, and its silence on Caesarion

segments.name: The Nile Fails, and the Barge on the Cydnus

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: the brother dead and the child crowned
stops.date_confidence: Corrected and tightened from the pool's loose 'mid-44 BC'. Wikipedia, 'Ptolemy XIV': alive by inscription on 26 July 44 BC, dead by August 44. Wikipedia, 'Caesarion' and 'Ptolemy XIV' both give 2 September 44 BC for the proclamation of Caesarion as co-ruler, aged three. The poisoning is not attested by any contemporary source and Wikipedia does not credit it to Josephus; the aconite is a modern conjecture. Recorded as an assumption, not a fact.
stops.campa: Ptolemy XIV is alive on the twenty-sixth of July, by an inscription, and dead by August. No source in antiquity states a cause. That she poisoned him is an assumption, made early and repeated since; the aconite is a later embellishment on the assumption. On the second of September the three-year-old Caesarion is proclaimed her co-ruler as Ptolemy XV Caesar, a colleague who cannot outvote her for fifteen years and whose title carries the name of the man Rome is at this moment turning into a god.
suggested_refs: Josephus, Against Apion 2.56-58, which charges her with killing a brother without naming the means

stops.name: Alexandria and the valley: the flood that does not come
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The low Nile floods of the mid-40s BC and the resulting famine and plague are argued from papyrology and from ice-core climate scholarship rather than narrated by any ancient source. The reported decree restricting grain movement from Upper Egypt toward Alexandria was not read in the original in preparing this file. Years approximate, month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The Nile floods badly several years running, and Egypt, which lives entirely off the flood, has famine and plague in the villages and price panic in the capital. A royal decree is reported that holds grain in Upper Egypt back from the market so that Alexandria eats first. That is the sort of thing the countryside remembers about Ptolemies. All of it stands on papyri and on ice cores rather than on any narrative, and the decree itself was not read here in the original.
sources: Research pool synthesis of papyrological and ice-core climate scholarship; no primary decree text verified
suggested_refs: Ice-core evidence for volcanic forcing and Nile flood failure in the 40s BC

stops.name: Tarsus, the Cydnus: Venus come to revel with Bacchus
stops.date_confidence: The summons and the meeting are attested to 41 BC; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01-01. The barge description is Plutarch, Life of Antony 26, fetched and quoted directly. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Tarsus pin, inherited byte-identical from pylades_of_cilicia.journey.json and apostle_paul.journey.json.
stops.campa: Antony, holding the East after Philippi, summons her to Cilicia to answer for having failed to help the assassins' cause. She takes her time and comes up the Cydnus at her own pace, on a barge with a gilded stern, purple sails and silver oars beating to flutes, lying under a gold canopy dressed as Aphrodite with boys costumed as Loves fanning her. Tarsus empties onto the riverbank until Antony is left sitting alone in the marketplace. The word going round the city is that Venus has come to revel with Bacchus for the good of Asia.
stops.quote: She herself reclined beneath a canopy spangled with gold, adorned like Venus in a painting, while boys like Loves in paintings stood on either side and fanned her.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 26, trans. Bernadotte Perrin (Loeb Classical Library), LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The Cydnus at Tarsus, now silted and shifted from its ancient course

stops.name: Ephesus, the Artemision: the sister taken from sanctuary
stops.date_confidence: The killing is broadly attested in the ancient tradition (Josephus, Appian, Dio) and is reported as done at Cleopatra's request; the exact legal mechanism is unknown and no source was fetched to the chapter in preparing this file. Month unknown, placed after Tarsus to order the segment. Whether Cleopatra was herself at Ephesus is not stated anywhere and is not claimed here.
stops.campa: Arsinoe IV, proclaimed queen against her during the Alexandrian war and then walked in chains through Caesar's triumph, has been living since as a suppliant in the sanctuary of Artemis at Ephesus. She is the last of the four royal children besides Cleopatra herself. Sanctuary in a temple is a protection every Greek city recognises, and the Artemision is the greatest sanctuary in Asia. At Cleopatra's asking, Antony sends men into the precinct. They kill her on the ground where she took refuge.
sources: World History Encyclopedia, 'Cleopatra VII', synthesising the Josephus and Appian traditions
suggested_refs: The Artemision at Ephesus and the ancient law of sanctuary for suppliants

stops.name: Aradus: the man who says he did not drown
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The episode is reported in the research pool as reflecting Appian, Civil Wars, but the passage could not be fetched to confirm chapter or wording, and no independent source was reached. Month and day are placed to order the segment only. Nothing places Cleopatra at Aradus herself.
stops.campa: On the island of Aradus off the Phoenician coast a man is living who says he is Ptolemy XIII, not drowned in the river after all. What the sources say came out of the Nile after the battle is a gilded corselet, and a corselet is room enough for a claim like this one. At her instigation Antony has him removed. The episode survives through one thin channel of report. Who he actually was, how long he had been saying it, and whether anyone on Aradus believed him, the record does not say.
sources: Research pool synthesis, probably reflecting Appian, Civil Wars; passage not fetched
suggested_refs: Appian, Civil Wars, on the Ptolemaic pretenders of the 40s BC

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: the Inimitable Livers
stops.date_confidence: Antony's wintering at Alexandria in 41/40 BC is attested (Livius.org). The Inimitable Livers material is Plutarch's Life of Antony, a standard citation from that Life, and was not refetched to the chapter here. The pearl anecdote is Pliny, Natural History 9.119-121, written roughly a century after the events, with no contemporary corroboration; recorded as tradition, not record.
stops.campa: Antony follows her back to Alexandria and winters there, and the two of them found a drinking society they call the Inimitable Livers: banquets, practical jokes, and nights walking the city in servants' clothes knocking on strangers' doors. The account is Plutarch's, written by a moralist who wants his reader to watch a Roman general dissolve. He also keeps her joke, made after she had a diver fasten a salted fish to Antony's line in front of the whole party. Pliny, later still, adds the wager and the pearl swallowed in vinegar.
stops.quote: Imperator, hand over thy fishing-rod to the fishermen of Pharos and Canopus; thy sport is the hunting of cities, realms, and continents.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 29, trans. Bernadotte Perrin (Loeb Classical Library), LacusCurtius; rendered as direct speech in Perrin and as reported speech in some other translations
sources: Plutarch, Life of Antony 29 (LacusCurtius) and the Inimitable Livers passages of the same Life
Pliny, Natural History 9.119-121, on the pearl
plinio_el_viejo.journey.json, for Pliny as the sole channel of the pearl anecdote
suggested_refs: plinio_el_viejo.journey.json
Pliny, Natural History book 9, on pearls and the luxury of the East

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: twins, and a wedding in Rome
stops.date_confidence: The twins' birth in 40 BC and Antony's marriage to Octavia in Rome in the same year are both attested; the month and day of the birth are unknown and defaulted to 01-01. That she did not contest the marriage is reconstruction from silence, not a documented position.
stops.campa: She bears twins and names them Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene, the sun and the moon, a Ptolemaic claim on the whole visible sky and a piece of eastern royal advertising aimed at people who can read it. Antony is not in Egypt for the birth. In the same year he patches up his quarrel with Octavian at Brundisium and seals the settlement by marrying Octavian's sister Octavia in Rome. Nothing survives of what Cleopatra said about that. She governs Egypt alone for the next three years.
suggested_refs: The Pact of Brundisium, 40 BC, and the marriage of Antony and Octavia

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: Herod at the queen's table
stops.date_confidence: Attested through Josephus, in the Jewish War and Antiquities, which the research pool cites and which was not refetched here. Month placed to order the segment. Josephus writes inside the Herodian tradition and is hostile to Cleopatra throughout, which affects the colouring of the meeting more than its occurrence.
stops.campa: Herod arrives at her court a fugitive, driven out of Judaea by a Parthian-backed rival, and she offers him a command in her own service. He declines it, sails on for Rome in winter, and comes back a king by decree of the Senate. The two of them will spend the next decade quarrelling over the balsam of Jericho, which she comes to own and he comes to farm. Everything known about the meeting comes from Josephus, who writes inside the Herodian tradition and gives the scene a charge of mutual calculation that suits him.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War and Jewish Antiquities, as characterised in the research pool; not refetched
flavius_josephus.journey.json, for Josephus as the hostile channel of the Cleopatra-Herod material
suggested_refs: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 15, on Cleopatra and Herod

stops.name: Antioch on the Orontes: the old Ptolemaic lands handed back
stops.date_confidence: The Antioch summons, the acknowledgement of the twins and the territorial grants are attested for 37 BC; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The exact extent of what was granted outright as against granted in revenue is disputed in the sources. Cyprus is included here with a caution: Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra' says only that 'the exact date at which Cyprus was returned to her control is not known, although she had a governor there by 42 BC', so the pool's confident 43 BC dating is not followed.
stops.campa: Antony summons her to Antioch, acknowledges the twins as his after four years, and hands over territory: parts of Phoenicia and Coele-Syria, stretches of Cilicia, Crete, Cyrenaica, and the balsam country of Judaea. Cyprus is already hers again, by an arrangement nobody dated. He is assembling an invasion of Parthia and needs money, grain and shipbuilding timber on a scale no other treasury in the East can meet. What the grants buy him is the Egyptian revenue. The army goes out the following year.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra' (fetched), on the undated return of Cyprus
suggested_refs: The Ptolemaic overseas empire before Rome dismantled it, and the extent of the 37 BC restoration

stops.name: Jericho: the balsam groves leased back to Herod
stops.date_confidence: The grant of the Jericho balsam and date revenues and the lease back to Herod are attested; her personal presence at Jericho is reported by Josephus and not independently confirmed, so the stop is a reconstruction as to her being there. Month placed to follow Antioch within the year. Josephus, Antiquities 15, was not refetched.
stops.campa: The Antioch grant carries the balsam groves and date palms of the Jericho plain, the richest agricultural ground in Judaea and the only place in the world where the balsam grows. She leases the concession back to Herod and spends the next decade extracting the rent from him. Josephus reports that she came to Judaea in person and met him there, and adds a scene of Herod being talked out of killing her by his own advisers. He is writing for a Herodian readership, and the scene should be held at arm's length.
sources: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 15, as cited in the research pool; not refetched
suggested_refs: The balsam plantations of Jericho and Ein Gedi, a royal monopoly under both Ptolemaic and Herodian control

stops.name: Leuke Kome, the Syrian coast: clothing for a beaten army
stops.date_confidence: The relief of the retreating army on the Syrian coast is attested and is a standard citation from Plutarch, Life of Antony 51, which was not refetched past the truncation point of the Penelope page consulted. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The coordinate is the stretch of coast between Berytus and Sidon and not a precisely located site.
stops.campa: The Parthian campaign she financed has ended with a third of the army gone, the whole siege train lost, and the cavalry destroyed. Antony brings what is left down out of the Armenian mountains in winter and stops on the Syrian coast between Berytus and Sidon, at a place with no harbour and no supplies of its own. She comes by sea with clothing and money for the survivors. Plutarch says the men were paid out of her ships. What she thought of the campaign she paid for, nobody recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Life of Antony 51 (standard citation, not refetched to the chapter)
suggested_refs: Antony's Parthian campaign of 36 BC and its retreat through Armenia

stops.name: Alexandria, the chancery: year sixteen, also year one
stops.date_confidence: The birth of Ptolemy Philadelphus in 36 BC is attested; month and day unknown. The double-dating of official documents as 'year 16, also year 1' is drawn from papyrological evidence summarised in the research pool and was not verified against a published papyrus here. The reading of the double date as a claim to a new era is interpretation, stated as such.
stops.campa: A third child is born, Ptolemy Philadelphus, named for the second Ptolemy, under whom the dynasty reached its widest extent. In the same period the chancery starts double-dating official documents: year sixteen, which is also year one. The count of her own reign runs on unbroken and a second count opens on top of it. No Egyptian practice requires this. The second count can be read as a claim that the kingdom she inherited and the kingdom Antony has handed back are two different kingdoms. It is a reading. The papyri themselves give two numbers and nothing else.
sources: Research pool synthesis of papyrological double-dating evidence
suggested_refs: Ptolemaic double-dated documents of 37/36 BC onward

stops.name: Alexandria, the Gymnasium: Queen of Kings
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia, 'Donations of Alexandria': 'gymnasium of Alexandria, autumn 34 BC... sat on golden thrones... Antony as Dionysus-Osiris, Cleopatra as Isis-Aphrodite'. The exact day is not recorded; 10-01 stands for the autumn. The preceding Armenian triumph through Alexandria with the captive Artavasdes II is attested in the same chronology.
stops.campa: In the gymnasium of Alexandria, on thrones set up on a platform, Antony sits as Dionysus and she sits as Isis, and the children are brought out dressed as the countries they are being given. Rome will hear that a Roman consul has given away the East. Caesarion is proclaimed King of Kings and son of the deified Julius; she is proclaimed Queen of Kings. Alexander Helios receives Armenia, Media and Parthia, which has not been conquered. Cleopatra Selene receives Cyrenaica. Ptolemy Philadelphus receives Syria and Cilicia. He is two years old.
suggested_refs: The Donations of Alexandria and their use in Octavian's propaganda of 33-32 BC

stops.name: Alexandria, the ordinance: one word in a second hand
stops.date_confidence: The papyrus is real and dated: P.Bingen 45, Berlin P. 25239, a royal ordinance granting tax privileges to a Roman absentee landlord, received at Alexandria 23 February 33 BC. The attribution of the subscription to Cleopatra's own hand is Peter van Minnen's argument from 2000 onward and is disputed: Bagnall, Derow and Sarri question whether the word is even in a different hand from the body, and since no signature of her name survives there is no palaeographic control. The research pool's transliteration 'ginesthoi' is not a real form and is corrected here to the Greek gamma-iota-nu-epsilon-sigma-theta-omega, ginestho.
stops.campa: A Roman absentee landlord petitions for exemption from Egyptian taxes on his estates, and the ordinance granting it is drawn up, copied out, and received at Alexandria. At the foot of the sheet a second hand has written one Greek word: let it be done. Peter van Minnen has argued the hand is hers, on the grounds that only the monarch could sign an edict into law and that the administrators circulating it would have known her writing. Other papyrologists doubt the word is in a second hand at all, and there is no signature of her name anywhere to compare it against.
stops.quote_source: P.Bingen 45 (Berlin P. 25239), royal ordinance received at Alexandria 23 February 33 BC, single word subscribed in a second hand; transliterated ginestho, 'let it be done'. Discussed by Jennifer Cromwell at papyrus-stories.com, summarising Peter van Minnen's attribution
sources: papyrus-stories.com, 'On a document signed by Cleopatra' (Jennifer Cromwell, 2020), summarising van Minnen
suggested_refs: P.Bingen 45 and the papyrological debate over whether Cleopatra's hand survives at all

segments.name: The War Declared Against a Woman

stops.name: Ephesus, the harbour: the client kings assemble
stops.date_confidence: The muster at Ephesus in 32 BC and the argument among Antony's officers about sending her home are attested in the Plutarchan narrative of the pre-Actium campaign, summarised in the research pool and not refetched to the chapter. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the harbour and city of Ephesus, distinct from the Artemision pin used earlier in this file.
stops.campa: Antony and Cleopatra concentrate at Ephesus: the fleet, the legions, and the client kings of the East with their contingents. She has brought ships and money, and she declines to go home. Several of Antony's Roman officers argue that she should be sent back to Egypt, not out of dislike but because her presence lets Octavian describe the war as a defence of Italy against a foreign queen, which is the only description under which Romans will readily fight other Romans. Antony keeps her with the army.
sources: Research pool synthesis of Plutarch's Antony on the pre-Actium muster; chapter not refetched
suggested_refs: Octavian's propaganda campaign of 33-32 BC, framing the war as against Egypt rather than against Antony

stops.name: Samos: a festival while the world is arming
stops.date_confidence: Standard citation from Plutarch's Life of Antony, not refetched past the truncation point of the source page consulted. Month is placed to order the segment between the Ephesus muster and the Athenian winter; no source dates the festival precisely.
stops.campa: The court moves to Samos and holds a festival. Kings send tribute, and actors, musicians and dancers are gathered in from across the Greek world to an island a season's sail from a war both sides know is coming. Plutarch sets it down as the last extravagance before the fall, which is what a biographer does with a party held in the spring of a year that ends badly. He is writing more than a century after the event, and he names no source for any of it.
sources: Plutarch, Life of Antony, Samos festival episode (standard citation, not refetched)
suggested_refs: The guild of the Artists of Dionysus, whose performers were summoned to Samos in 32 BC

stops.name: Athens: honours for the queen, a divorce for the wife
stops.date_confidence: The wintering at Athens in 32/31 BC and the Athenian honours to Cleopatra are attested in the ancient hostile tradition, summarised in the research pool. The divorce is corrected: the pool placed Antony's separation from Octavia in 37 BC, which contradicts its own later entry and the record. Wikipedia, 'Mark Antony' gives the marriage as 40-32 BC and Wikipedia, 'War of Actium' has him marrying Cleopatra in 32 BC before divorcing Octavia. Month placed to order the segment.
stops.campa: They winter at Athens, where the city votes her the honours it had voted Octavia when Octavia lived here as Antony's wife. In Rome in the same months the triumviral powers lapse, both consuls and a large body of senators leave the city to join Antony, and Antony sends Octavia formal notice of divorce after twelve years of marriage. Octavian then reads out in the Senate a document he says is Antony's will, and Rome declares war on the queen of Egypt. Antony's name is kept out of the declaration.
suggested_refs: The reading of Antony's alleged will in the Senate, 32 BC

stops.name: Cape Actium: sixty ships and the open sea
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 2 September 31 BC. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 38.943/20.7346 to Wikipedia, 'Battle of Actium' (38.92500 N, 20.72500 E), about 2.1 km away; the pool's own note quoted the correct figure and then recorded a different one. The pool's 'broke through the line' is also softened: Wikipedia has her squadron in the rear, retreating 'to the open sea without engaging', and Antony following because he believed 'it was mere panic and all was lost'.
stops.campa: Her squadron of about sixty ships lies at the back of the line with the treasury aboard and the sails stowed on deck, which no fleet expecting a full day's fighting does. In the afternoon the wind turns, she puts up sail and goes out through the gap without engaging, running south. Antony leaves his flagship, takes a five-banked ship and follows her, believing the day already lost. The fleet he leaves behind fights until evening and then surrenders, and the legions waiting on shore surrender a week later without a battle.
suggested_refs: The Actium victory monument raised by Octavian at Nikopolis, with its captured ship rams

stops.name: Alexandria, the Great Harbour: the fleet comes home dressed as victory
stops.date_confidence: The staging of a victory on the return and the winter of negotiations are attested in the Plutarchan and Dio narratives, summarised in the research pool. Month approximate. The competing versions of what she offered Octavian, abdication for her children, money, or Antony's exile, are not reconcilable and are left standing as they are.
stops.campa: She brings the ships into the Great Harbour with garlands up and the flutes playing, so that Alexandria hears a victory before it hears anything else, and moves at once against anyone in the city likely to act on the truth. Antony comes back separately and sits for a while on the seaward side refusing to see people. Envoys go to Octavian through the winter carrying offers: her abdication in favour of her children, money, Antony sent into exile. The accounts of what was offered and what was answered do not agree.
sources: Research pool synthesis of Plutarch and Cassius Dio on the post-Actium negotiations
suggested_refs: The competing ancient accounts of the Alexandria negotiations of 31/30 BC

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace: the head sent to Media
stops.date_confidence: Date corrected from the pool's 'probably 30 BCE'. Wikipedia, 'Artavasdes II of Armenia': he 'died in 31 BC when Cleopatra had him decapitated following Antony's defeat at the Battle of Actium', and she sent the head to Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene to secure his support. Month unknown, placed after Actium. The whole episode rests on Cassius Dio, writing some two and a half centuries later, with no second witness.
stops.campa: The king of Armenia has been held in Alexandria since Antony paraded him through the city in silver chains, and with the war lost he is worth nothing as a hostage and something as a gift. She has him beheaded and sends the head to Artavasdes of Media Atropatene, whose support is still worth buying. It is the last recorded act of foreign policy of the Ptolemaic kingdom, and all of it comes from Cassius Dio, writing some two and a half centuries later, with no second witness anywhere.
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History, as cited in the research pool
suggested_refs: Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene and the shifting Armenian-Median alignments after Actium

stops.name: Clysma on the Red Sea: ships dragged across the sand
stops.date_confidence: The ship-hauling and the Nabataean burning are standard citations from Plutarch's Life of Antony; her own presence at the haul site is not stated in any source and is not claimed here. Month approximate, spring 30 BC. Coordinate is the canonical atlas head-of-the-Red-Sea pin, inherited byte-identical from strabo.journey.json, where it stands for Arsinoe on the Red Sea.
stops.campa: She orders ships hauled overland from the Nile to the head of the Red Sea, meaning to put a fleet and a treasury beyond Octavian's reach and, if it can be managed, outside the Roman world altogether. The road she is trying to reopen is the one Egypt had used for centuries to reach India. The Nabataeans burn the ships on the beach, put up to it, the reports say, by Octavian through Herod. Whether she was at the water herself when the news came, or in Alexandria, no source says.
sources: Plutarch, Life of Antony, ship-hauling episode (standard citation, not refetched)
strabo.journey.json, stop 'Arsinoe on the Red Sea, the fleet he does not sail with', for the coordinate
suggested_refs: The Ptolemaic canal and portage routes between the Nile and the Red Sea, and their Roman reuse

stops.name: Alexandria, the mausoleum: treasure and kindling in one room
stops.date_confidence: The mausoleum, its position beside the palace, and the treasure and combustibles moved into it are attested in Plutarch's account. The building's exact site is lost to later construction and to subsidence, so the coordinate is the palace pin used throughout this file rather than an independent location. Month approximate, spring or early summer 30 BC.
stops.campa: Beside the palace she finishes a tomb for herself and moves the treasure of the kingdom into it: gold, silver, pearls, ebony, ivory, cinnamon, and a quantity of firewood and tow laid in among it all. The arrangement is legible to anyone who wants the money, and the man who wants the money is Octavian, who has an army to pay off. She can burn it, and while it can be burned she holds one thing worth negotiating over. From inside the building, with the doors shut and the tow lying among the ivory, she goes on sending out envoys.
sources: Research pool synthesis of Plutarch's account of the mausoleum
suggested_refs: The submerged and built-over royal quarter of Alexandria, in which the mausoleum has never been located

stops.name: Alexandria, outside the walls: the last cavalry morning
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the final chapters of Plutarch's Life of Antony, summarised in the research pool; the skirmish is dated 31 July 30 BC and the defection of the fleet and cavalry to the following morning. Coordinate is the open ground immediately outside the ancient city and is approximate.
stops.campa: On the last day of July Antony takes out what cavalry he has, meets Octavian's horse outside the walls and beats them, and comes back into the palace still in armour to tell her about it. In the morning his fleet rows out of the harbour, raises oars in salute to the enemy, and joins them. The cavalry goes over in the same hour. He is left with infantry that will not fight, in a city that has already decided, and he says aloud that she has sold him.
sources: Research pool synthesis of Plutarch, Life of Antony, final chapters
suggested_refs: The defection of Antony's fleet and cavalry at Alexandria, 1 August 30 BC

stops.name: Alexandria, the mausoleum: hauled up through the window
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1 August 30 BC. Wikipedia, 'Death of Cleopatra', summarising Plutarch: Antony 'stabbed himself through the stomach with a sword... carried to Cleopatra's tomb, where he died in her presence'. The false report of her death, the slave Eros, and the sealed doors are Plutarch's, chapters 76-77, which were not independently retrieved to the chapter in preparing this file.
stops.campa: Word reaches him that she is dead, which she is not: she has shut herself into the tomb with two waiting-women and sent out a message he reads as final. He asks his slave Eros to kill him and Eros kills himself instead, so Antony does it himself, through the stomach, badly, and does not die of it. Then the correction arrives. They carry him to the mausoleum, where the doors have been sealed and cannot be opened, and the three women haul him up on ropes through an upper window.
sources: Plutarch, Life of Antony 76-77 (not independently retrieved; flagged as a gap)
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Antony 76-77, on Eros and the sealed tomb

stops.name: Alexandria, the mausoleum: Caesar's heir at the door
stops.date_confidence: The capture through the window, the interview, and the scene with the steward Seleucus are attested in Plutarch, Life of Antony 83 and in Cassius Dio, Roman History 51.12, both fetched via Perseus and LacusCurtius. The exact day of the interview is not recorded and 08-08 orders the segment between Antony's death and hers. Dio and Plutarch give different exchanges for what may be the same meeting; both are recorded and neither is preferred.
stops.campa: Octavian's men get in through the window while an envoy keeps her talking at the door, and she is taken alive before she can use the dagger. He comes to see her a few days later. She has torn her breast in mourning and she is feverish, and she goes through the inventory of her treasure with him; when her steward Seleucus points out that she has held items back, she strikes him across the face in front of the Roman and explains the omission as gifts meant for Octavia and Livia. He tells her to be of good cheer and lets it pass.
stops.quote: Hail, master, for Heaven has granted you the mastery and taken it from me.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 51.12, trans. Earnest Cary (Loeb Classical Library), LacusCurtius; her greeting to Octavian at their meeting after the fall of Alexandria
sources: Plutarch, Life of Antony 83 (fetched, Perseus Digital Library)
suggested_refs: The two irreconcilable ancient versions of the Octavian interview, in Plutarch and in Dio

stops.name: Alexandria, the mausoleum: the basket of figs
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra' gives '10 or 12 August 30 BC' and Livius.org gives 12 August; the variation follows from calendar conversion and is not resolved here. The mechanism is contradicted across the earliest surviving sources and is left contradicted. Strabo is the earliest of them and was alive at the time, though writing later and in Alexandria only from about 26 BC; that he is the earliest surviving reporter of the alternatives is stated in the research pool and not in strabo.journey.json's own text.
stops.campa: She bathes, eats, and has a basket of figs carried in past the guards, who look into it and let it through. Then she dresses in full regalia and lies down on a gold couch with Iras at her feet and Charmion at her head. When the guards break in, Iras is dead and Charmion is straightening the diadem before falling herself. What killed her is not settled. Strabo, the earliest of the surviving reporters, gives an asp or a poisoned ointment as alternatives; Plutarch has the asp in the figs and also a hollow implement; Dio has small puncture marks and a needle.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 86, trans. Bernadotte Perrin (Loeb Classical Library), Perseus Digital Library; her words on finding the asp among the figs
sources: Wikipedia, 'Death of Cleopatra' (fetched), summarising Strabo, Plutarch, Cassius Dio and Suetonius
Plutarch, Life of Antony 84 and 86 (fetched, Perseus)
strabo.journey.json, for Strabo's Alexandrian residence from 26 BC
suggested_refs: The lost memoir of the physician Olympos, which Plutarch says he used and which does not survive
Suetonius on Octavian's Psylli snake-charmers, called in to draw out the venom

stops.name: Alexandria, the royal burial: laid beside him in royal fashion
stops.date_confidence: The permission for the burial is attested in Plutarch and Dio; neither names the place. Day is set two days after the death to order the segment and is not recorded anywhere. The tomb has never been securely located: Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra' gives the infobox entry 'Unlocated tomb (probably in Egypt)'. Kathleen Martinez's Taposiris Magna hypothesis is not staged as a stop here because the excavating is hers, not Cleopatra's; it is carried in the references instead.
stops.campa: Octavian, who wanted her alive for the triumph and did not get her, allows the burial to go as she asked for it: laid beside Antony, in royal fashion, with her women buried honourably too. The funeral of the last Ptolemy goes forward by permission of the man who has just taken the kingdom. Plutarch records the permission and so does Dio. Neither of them says where. No excavation since has produced the tomb, and the royal quarter in which it would have stood has gone under the sea or under the modern city.
stops.quote: Dear Antony, I buried thee but lately with hands still free; now, however, I pour libations for thee as a captive, and so carefully guarded that I cannot either with blows or tears disfigure this body of mine, which is a slave's body, and closely watched that it may grace the triumph over thee
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 84, trans. Bernadotte Perrin (Loeb Classical Library), Perseus Digital Library; her lament at Antony's tomb, spoken days before her own death
sources: Wikipedia, 'Taposiris Magna' (fetched): 'No definitive evidence of Cleopatra's actual burial has been confirmed'
suggested_refs: Kathleen Martinez's excavations at the Osiris temple of Taposiris Magna since 2002, which have produced Ptolemaic tombs, coins bearing her image and a 1,305-metre tunnel, and no artefact naming either ruler
Franck Goddio's underwater survey of the submerged royal quarters and Antirhodos, 1996-2003

stops.name: Alexandria, the Caesareum: a province, and a temple finished by the victor
stops.date_confidence: Caesarion's flight toward the Red Sea, his recall through his tutor Rhodon and his killing are attested, as is the sparing of the three children by Antony and their appearance in Octavian's triumph; no source gives an exact date, and 08-29 orders the close of the file. That the Caesareum was begun or substantially developed under Cleopatra and completed under Augustus is attested, its original dedication debated. The obelisks were moved there around 13-12 BC, after her death; that reach past her own clock is why it is stated as the building's later history and not as a scene. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from hypatia.journey.json.
stops.campa: Caesarion, seventeen, has been sent up the Red Sea road with his tutor Rhodon, who talks him into turning back, and Octavian has him killed. The three children by Antony are spared, taken to Rome, and walked in the triumph. Egypt becomes a province and is held by the emperor in person, and the grain of the valley goes to feed the city that took it. The temple she began for the deified Julius is finished by his heir, and two obelisks a thousand years older than either of them are brought down and set up at its door.
sources: Wikipedia, "Cleopatra's Needle" (fetched), on the Caesareum and the obelisks moved there c. 13-12 BC
hypatia.journey.json, which records the Caesareum standing in Alexandria in 415 CE
suggested_refs: The Caesareum of Alexandria, later converted into a cathedral, and the pair of obelisks that carried her name to London and New York
Cleopatra Selene II as queen of Mauretania at Caesarea, minting as 'Queen Cleopatra' a generation after Actium
